Round One: Depends on where they are, and which characters they replace. If they replace some of the non-Nedry staff, there's an excellent chance that many of them are eaten before Hammond invites the inspectors. If they replace the inspectors + kids (Everyone who goes out in the cars), they die by Tyrannosaurus, at least assuming that in this universe they haven't seen Jurassic Park because they're living it. If any of them replace Nedry, dinosaurs never happen because the computers can't deal with the lines of DNA. Alternatively, if they replace Nedry right at the start of the movie events, then everyone goes on fine because the dinosaurs don't get out. Round Two: Depends on how these guys are housed, which DNA version of Linkin Park they are, and whether there is a Nedry to sabotage everything. If these guys are housed by member, such that all of the Chesters or all of the Mikes are in the same enclosure, then it is much less likely that there will be the sort of cohesion and teamwork that is shown in Linkin Park. If they are housed by band, such that each enclosure has a full band, perhaps told to play a different song per enclosure, then some team work might be done. First things first, with instruments come instruments accessories. Guitar and mic cables can be turned into rope if push comes to shove, and may be able to be used to create shorts in the electric fences to allow escape. Unfortunately for the Linkin Parks, if they don't take out the cameras, they will quickly be discovered to not be in their cages since they can't breed more of themselves (The cameras are pretty much only good at counting the number of animals you expect.). Another point of contention is that probably not all of the Linkin Parks are equal. There is Linkin Park Prime, who presumably is not a part of the park, and is the original Linkin Park DNA. In the book, because of the incompleteness of the DNA, there are different versions of the dinosaurs, with each new version being a "more complete" batch of DNA. For example, the raptors are on Version 4.0. Given the amount of time it takes to create adult humans, there are probably many versions of Linkin Park in the park, ranging from newborns with the best DNA of the lot, to adults who are probably retarded. This is a major disadvantage for the Linkin Parks. Finally, Round Two belongs to the Linkin Parks, as Linkin Park Prime would force everyone off the island with a cease and desist. Round Three: After the hullabaloo of Round Two, Linkin Park scientists have decided to do something extraordinary and not against any law yet. They have decided to take their current DNA batches, and combine them with some external reference to dinosaur DNA. After a quick Google, there are 6 members of Linkin Park. There were 6 major dinos in Jurassic Park. Let's match them up. * Chester (lead vocals) - T. rex (lead dinosaur, awesome roar) * Rob (drums) - Brachiosaurus (because they boom when they walk) * Brad (guitar) - Dilophosaurus * Dave (bass) - Gallimimus * Joe (electronics) - Triceratops * Mike (keys) - Velociraptor With these combinations, weirdly enough, only the behavior came through, except for the Bradilophosaurs who spit poison. Honestly, I'm going to give this one to the Linkin Parks because a 40' tall Chesterex with that sort of voice would probably drive everyone off on its own. Also, unless the caretakers prepare for the size of an 85' Robrachiosaur, those will be able to break the fences for everyone since these guys still have enough human intelligence for music and murder. Round Four - Dinosaurs take it so hard. Round Five -  Normal raptors are going to be the real threat. The rest of the dinos, except the Gallis, are probably taken out by their respective Linkin Park members. If the raptors work together with the T. rex to take down Chesterex, a la Jurassic World, then the dinosaurs will win by having the T. rex for other matchups. Best case for Linkin Park is if the big guys focus on the raptors, and maybe the T. rex, although I believe Chesterex can take T. rex in 1v1. Probably 7/10 to dinosaurs.

Well, you have to remember that a major social media platform was not invented in a bubble. Social networks have always been a thing in real life, and when people came online, those followed. Before the true social networking sites came online, you still had people connecting together via chat rooms and message boards. Email clients and such had contact cards that you filled out with your contacts' information for the real world. Eventually, websites that people actually call social networking websites started to appear. One early example was an early social network, but the big one was a popular early social network. That platform pretty much gave everyone who signed up a website, and allowed people to link to their friends' websites. It also had an embedded music player that was great for bands, so a lot of groups used it for promotion. The biggest complaints with that platform were that users had too much control over their profiles that usually used terrible CSS and autoplaying embedded media to make some really cringy profiles, and that predators used the site to try to find kids. An online wiki has a decent writeup about that platform. A major social network came along near the height of that platform's popularity, but it focused initially on exclusivity, with only college students at a few colleges and universities being able to join. That major network lowered that bar as time went on. Compared to the early platform, the major network avoided the user-caused UI problem by not allowing CSS modifications to user profiles. Instead, users could fill out information about themselves in blurbs that still exist on the site today (About Me). The major network also avoided the predator problem during its startup years with the exclusivity thing. As for how it became the biggest site in the world, that's mostly just because it eventually reached a tipping point where it became essential, like email. That major network for most people is still a pretty great way to communicate with friends, especially once group messages became a thing. It's also pretty easy to find people on it, provided you have a mutual friend with them. The major network also has generally bought out any competition that actually looks dangerous to them, like a messaging app. Other social sites and apps are examples of websites that took the cool factor away from the major network, but their users still have profiles on the major network.
